name: Math Mammoth
line: Math Mammoth teaches by worktext and chapter. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Math Mammoth: a worktext the adult places, checks and reviews. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Math Mammoth is a set of worktexts: a learner reads a lesson, works the exercises on paper and takes a test at the end of each chapter, and the adult checks the work and decides what comes next [1][2]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Math Mammoth places a learner with an end-of-year test for a grade, scored against percent cutoffs [3]. From there the learner follows the book's order, with a test at the end of each chapter [2].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In Math Mammoth a learner works the exercises on paper. The learner or the adult checks them against the answer key, and the adult decides what to do about a mistake [2]. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, of mixed ages and subjects, feedback that explains had the largest average effect, 0.49, against 0.05 for marking right or wrong only [11].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Math Mammoth the unit is the lesson in the book: a few pages of explanation, worked examples and visual models, then a set of exercises [1][5]. Videos go with many lessons [6].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Math Mammoth's chapters are built for mastery and end in a test, with no stated rule for what counts as mastered [2]. Gaps are filled with its Blue Series, topic books the adult chooses and puts in order [4].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Math Mammoth ends each chapter with a mixed review lesson, has cumulative review sheets, and offers separate spiral review workbooks. The adult decides when to use them [1][2]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [12].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus in one program. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. Math Mammoth places a learner at a grade, with section scores to spot gaps [3]. Its complete curriculum runs from kindergarten through grade 8 and does not offer algebra 1 or above [1].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 8. No algebra 1 or above [1].
rows.start: End-of-year placement tests for each grade, with percent cutoffs and section scores to spot gaps [3].
rows.teaching: Worktext lessons written to the student, with worked examples and visual models [1][5]. Videos for many lessons [6].
rows.next: The next lesson in the book. The adult decides what to add, skip or review [2].
rows.mastery: Mastery-based chapters, each ending in a test. No rule for mastery stated [2].
rows.review: A mixed review lesson per chapter, cumulative review sheets and separate spiral review workbooks. The adult times them [1][2].
rows.print: PDF books to print, with answer keys and tests [1]. The same book for every learner.
rows.adult: Plans the schedule, checks answers with the key, gives chapter tests, and chooses when to add review [2].
rows.reports: None found in the pages we read. The adult grades by hand with the answer key [2].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [8][9][10].

theirs: Math Mammoth is a series of math worktexts written by Maria Miller, who holds a master's degree in mathematics and began writing after tutoring homeschoolers [5]. The complete curriculum, the Light Blue Series, runs from kindergarten through grade 8 [1]. The Blue Series holds the same lessons sorted by topic, for filling gaps or building a custom course [4]. Miller writes that visual models work much like manipulatives, before a learner moves to abstract work [5].

A lesson is a few pages written to the student: an explanation, worked examples and visual models, then exercises on paper [1][2]. Each chapter centers on one theme and ends with a mixed review and a test [2]. The adult plans the schedule, checks the work with the answer key and decides what to add [2].
credit: Lessons written to the student. The author writes that students can often read and study them on their own [2].
Visual models before abstract work [5]. A What Works Clearinghouse guide rates concrete and semi-concrete representations as strong evidence for elementary math intervention [13].
A mixed review lesson at the end of every chapter [2].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Math Mammoth on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports. Evidence for ESSA lists it without a rating, because no studies met its inclusion requirements [8]. The What Works Clearinghouse has no intervention report on it [9]. The home page cites no research [10].
Its testimonials page carries parent and teacher stories, some with one child's test scores. None that we read has a comparison group [7].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, of mixed ages and subjects, feedback that explains had the largest average effect, 0.49, against 0.05 for marking right or wrong only [11]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [12]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want math from a book, on paper, with an adult who teaches from it and checks the work.
amp: You want every answer checked and explained as it is given.
You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or ready for algebra.
You want paper workbooks made from your learner's own record.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Math Mammoth?
questions.answer: In Math Mammoth a learner reads a lesson and works exercises on paper, and the adult checks them with the answer key and decides what comes next [2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Math Mammoth work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of Math Mammoth on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [8][9][10].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. A learner can read lessons from the worktext and practice in AMP, which places them from their first answers.
